text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

The Wallis inquiry into the financial system yesterday released a comprehensive discussion paper which suggested the possibility of removing guarantees on bank deposits. The paper also recommended the payments system be thrown open to non-bank financial institutions in order to boost competition. Page 1.

Auscert is called in at pre-Christmas time to fix up to 60 computer break-ins each month. Graham Rees of Auscert believes the increase in hacker activity around Christmas is due to students being on holiday and "loonies" having more time on their hands. Speakers at a two-day conference in Sydney, titled Information Warfare, have called for greater attention to be paid to the issue and for Australia to gather better statistics and to raise public awareness. Page 2.

Following a warning from Treasurer Peter Costello that the federal government would respond to Senate votes against budget measures by putting them to the Upper House again in three months - triggering a dissolution of both Houses of Parliament - Prime Minister John Howard quickly rejected the suggestion last night, saying he wanted Parliament to run full term. Page 3.

According to the Department of Industrial Relations' report, Wage Trends in Enterprise Bargaining, wages growth through enterprise bargaining slowed in the past quarter but private sector workers gained average wage rises of 5.3 percent a year, down from 6.1 percent in the previous quarter. Page 5.
THE AUSTRALIAN

Prime Minister John Howard was last night forced to rule out threats of an early election made yesterday by Treasurer Peter Costello. Howard said he wanted the Coalition to run its full term and had no intention of tax increases. The press conference was called after Costello hinted a double dissolution may result from the Senate rejecting government budget bills. Page 1.

The federal government's review of the financial system has pledged a "better deal" for consumers and hinted at benefits for small business. The inquiry's chairman, Stan Wallis, yesterday released a discussion paper which opened up the possibility of a radical shake-up of the banking and finance sector. Page 1.

Reserve Bank Governor Ian Macfarlane has opposed the ACTU's "living wage" claim, branding it as inflationary and putting jobs at risk. While opposing the claim to boost award payments by up to 8.75 percent, MacFarlane backed the government's propsed safety net wage increase for low-income workers. Page 1.

South Australia's new Premier John Olsen has suggested there may be a front bench reshuffle before Christmas. After being sworn in as the state's new leader, less than 24 hours after a party-room vote saw Liberal leader Dean Brown defeated, Olsen said his government would focus on jobs growth and small business. Page 2.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

The federal government's inquiry into the financial system, chaired by Stan Wallis, has recommended bank customers should make their deposits "completely safe" by taking out a form of deposit insurance, because the inquiry found most Australians wrongly believed their savings are fully protected by the Reserve Bank. Page 1.

Australian Republican Movement chairman Malcolm Turnbull has accused the federal government of abandoning an election platform on the republic issue, claiming next year's proposed Constitutional Convention is simply a placebo. Turnbull has also backed charges by former Prime Minister Paul Keating that the current federal government had no intention of allowing Australia to become a republic. Page 1.

For the first time, New South Wales parents will receive detailed information regarding the performance of government schools as part of new school report cards. The report cards, due for release from the second term next year, will contain information about the schools' comparative performance in key areas such as English, maths and science. Page 1.

Holden is suffering a huge embarrassment with the recall of nearly 300,000 of its latest model Commodores being forced upon it by the model's serious engine problems, faulty service parts, sound systems that do not work and defective anti-theft keys. Page 1.
THE AGE

Victorian Premier Jeff Kennett has arrived back in Australia from an eight-day tour of Asia and thrown his full determination behind his contentious review of the auditor-general's office, yesterday lashing out at his own back bench. The review is to confirm whether state government departments should appoint their own auditors. Page A1.

Prime Minister John Howard yesterday confirmed that his government would serve its full term in office, rejecting Treasurer Peter Costello's earlier threat of an early election and new taxes over the Senate's blocking of key revenue measures. Howard said he had always believed that Parliament should run its full term. Page A1.

The Australian police force has been given a great boost with the release of the latest Bureau of Statistics survey results stating 70 percent of people said they were satisfied with police services and only nine percent were dissatisfied. The survey also found eight percent of Australian homes had a modem and 36 percent had at least one mobile phone. Page A3.

The Melbourne City Council's election earlier this year might have been very different had more than 1000 postal votes which arrived on the Monday after the close of voting been counted. A report on the poll suggests these votes may have been counted in at least two wards where the margins were tight. Page A3.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
